title: Biohacking Muscle Growth with Nucleus Overload
summary: NH's complete guide to nucleus overload (NO), based on 1.5 years of running it for his lats. NO means very low-intensity, high-volume, high-frequency isolation work for small lagging muscles, done as supersets in dead rest time, far from failure and progressed by reps, sets and days rather than load. He covers programming rules, a step-by-step example and the best NO exercises for each muscle group.
claims: Muscle grows either by enlarging cells (hypertrophy) or by adding cells (hyperplasia); he does not care which, only whether the muscle grows
Nucleus overload works mainly through hyperplasia, adding satellite cells through metabolic stress rather than breaking down muscle fibre
You do not need to know the science of how a muscle grows to grow it; the theory is only the cherry on top
He has run NO for his lats for about 1.5 years and for his calves for 6 months; the lat results convinced him it works
He plans to run NO for every lagging muscle: lats, calves, forearms and triceps
Small muscles usually lag because lifters cannot fit enough work for them into the program, not because they fail to respond
NO only makes sense once you have already trained the lagging muscle properly with hard sets and it still will not grow
NO uses volume and frequency as the growth drivers while intensity stays irrelevantly low; it is junk volume by design, and if it becomes quality volume it is no longer NO
Never reach failure on NO; you should always have at least 5 reps left, and being stopped by failure means you did too many reps or chose too heavy a weight
Chasing failure in a low-intensity window wastes time and only adds more low-quality volume
NO is cost-efficient because it costs very little energy and does not hurt the rest of the program, but it is not time-efficient
Always program NO as supersets placed in dead rest time, never as straight sets; it barely fatigues the muscle, the cardiovascular system or the CNS
NO suits small muscles: they get little work from compounds, have low work capacity and a shallow baseline, and recover fast (a small bucket empties and refills quickly)
Big muscles are poor NO candidates: compounds already fatigue them, their endurance baseline is deep (NO for hamstrings is like digging a ditch someone keeps refilling), and they recover more slowly
NO cannot replace hard sets; it is a complement, just as supplements cannot replace solid food
NO counts toward tonnage but low-quality tonnage; 4000 lb of low-quality work might be worth only about 400 lb of high-quality work
NO does not carry over to strength; trying to overload NO with load turns it into hard sets, a mistake he made himself, so add weight only rarely
The same exercise can serve as both a hard set and NO with different parameters: he does heavy pullovers with 90-95 lb for 12 and NO pullovers with 60 lb for 7-10 reps far from failure
Do not do NO for a muscle on days it already gets hard sets (e.g. lat NO on heavy chin-up day); training agonists with hard sets and NO on the same day is suboptimal
He does NO pull-ups and NO pullovers on the same day, which he admits is suboptimal but suits his preference
Done right, NO takes only 2-3% out of the recovery bucket; take 10-20% and your hard sets suffer, and because it is high-frequency, the small amounts add up to a lot of tonnage over a year
Watch for overuse injuries and strength loss; if hard sets start to suffer, you have made NO a priority, which is a mistake
NO should only tickle the muscle and feel like nothing happened; no pump is needed
Use isolation movements only for NO; compounds cause diffuse fatigue, risk injury through Bulgarian-style overload and become limited by cardio
When programming for bodybuilding, place compounds first and isolation after, because compounds like the deadlift take the most space and affect the days around them
Use one isolation movement per muscle for NO, or two at most if experienced and closely related (e.g. lat pulldown and straight-arm pulldown or pullover)
Repeatability test: a second NO set should match the first without effort (e.g. 30 reps of triceps extensions twice); with hard sets, matching reps means the first set was not hard enough
Progress NO by adding reps first, then sets, then days, and add weight last
NO is the cherry on top, a very small share of quality tonnage; do not let the whole program turn into an NO fest of junk volume
Spread NO over as many days and slots as possible and rotate exercises instinctively whenever you feel like it, which you could not do with compounds
NO should be mindless work: no focus, no pump, no mind-muscle connection, so it never becomes mentally taxing and you never dodge it
Never create a dedicated NO day; only use spaces in days you already train

Example cycle: triceps extensions on Monday and Friday after squats and rows, 4 sets of 15 with 25 lb; add reps until it gets time-inefficient, then add slots, then other days, and only add weight once every day is capped
For the lats, high-volume, high-frequency pullovers and pull-ups work: pick a weight you could do 25 times, do 7-10 reps for 3-4 sets 2-3 times a week, and give it a year
Grease the groove for pull-ups is essentially nucleus overload
For calves, NO with standing and seated raises at 10-15 reps, multiplying sets and days, is the best way to train them; heavy calf work has a place but should not be the bulk
NO is around 30% intensity, so you can do it hungover, tired or depressed, because strength does not matter
Welders and arm wrestlers have the biggest forearms outside bodybuilding because of huge volume; train forearms with wrist and finger curls, and finger curls fixed his wrist pain

Grippers work well for forearm NO at 2-3 times a week, 3-4 sets of medium reps; do dead hangs away from failure or 1-2 times a week after lower body, since holds can hurt grip strength unless you use straps
For trap NO, shrugs for 10-15 reps, 3-4 sets, 3 times a week will blow up the traps
For triceps NO use extensions (bench, overhead cable), not close-grip bench; done intelligently it will not hurt pressing
For shoulder NO use rear delt flies and lateral raises, never presses
Abs are best trained every day with a few non-fatiguing sets of crunches or leg raises
For neck NO use neck curls, not neck bridges, which carry too much fatigue
For biceps NO use elastic band curls; dumbbell or barbell curls at high frequency tend to cause biceps tendonitis

If you insist on NO for big muscles: leg extensions for quads, leg curls for hamstrings, hip thrusts for glutes, flies or ring flies for chest, ring rows or dumbbell rows at 40-50% of max for mid back, static bridges for lower back
NO is not for beginners, who have nothing but weak points and should focus on hard sets; it is for late novices onward, and a late novice should do it for only one muscle
Never replace hard-set volume with NO; bodybuilders who only do irrelevant sets look like garbage when they are not on drugs
Start with a single NO cycle so the boredom does not put you off; once it proves itself, add more; NO is a project that takes years
exercises: heavy for hard sets; light (weight you could do 25 times) for 7-10 reps in NO
forearm NO; fixed his wrist pain
stop before failure, or 1-2x/wk at end of lower day
forearms, but very fatiguing and can impair grip

shoulder NO with low joint cost

keep shoulder and triceps out of it, away from failure
chest NO without pec tendon risk
mid-back NO; DB row has a great stimulus-to-fatigue ratio
lower back NO, though it makes little sense
